subtopic: REPORTS AS TO ISSUE OF USED UNIFORMS TO CANADIAN ARMY

speechtext: On the order for motions:

speakeroldname: Hon. BROOKE CLAXTON (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: REPORTS AS TO ISSUE OF USED UNIFORMS TO CANADIAN ARMY
speechtext:
In view of the general interest I should like to give an oral reply to three questions put to me by the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) with regard to the summer clothing of the Canadian army.
Early in 1947 action was initiated to obtain a summer uniform for the army of a type similar to that already authorized for the R.C.A.F. Upon investigation it was found that a suitable tropical worsted cloth could not be produced in adequate quantities at that time. It was however definitely decided that tropical worsted uniforms would be issued to the Canadian army (active) and this will be done as soon as the cloth can be manufactured and the uniforms made. Contract demands for this purpose have already been issued but delivery will not commence before late summer. No second-hand R.C.A.F. khaki drill uniforms have been or will be issued to the Canadian army. During the war some 200,000 khaki drill uniforms were obtained from the R.C.A.F. for the purpose of clothing Canadian troops in Italy but were never shipped. These were not worn uniforms and were to all intents and purposes the same as the army khaki uniform which was and is standard issue. To scrap these and all other khaki drill uniforms at the end of the war would have seriously upset the supply of cloth for essential civilian and military needs. Even after the issue of tropical worsted uniforms, khaki drill will still be used for active training in field conditions.

I should like to add a word to what has been said already in reference to this bill. Already the committee has listened with interest to the remarks of the Minister of Veterans Affairs and other hon. members who have expressed their views. The purpose of this bill is to authorize increases in the basic rates of pension. Certain other minor amendments of an administrative nature are also incorporated. It will be noted that section 1 deals with the permanent force, but in all the discussion that has taken place thus far no reference has been made to permanent force cases. I am exercising my prerogative to bring to the attention of the minister one case which has been brought to me within the last few days.
This is the case of a permanent force veteran who served in both world wars; and I mention it because I believe there are many similar cases which should receive attention. The veteran's name is Leonard Tritsch, and his number was P-8964. He is an ex-sergeant of the R.C.H.A. Friends of his brought the case to my attention, and I have taken it up with the minister. This man served in the Royal Garrison Artillery of the imperial army from 1906 to 1919, during which time he had active service in England and France. After world war I, he enlisted in the R.C.H.A. in Canada and served from 1926 until 1939, when he joined the active service and served until his discharge on November 13, 1946, being later assessed as a one hundred per cent disability. On discharge his service pension, after twenty years of service, entitled him to $8925.
I emphasize the words "service pension." This veteran suffered a stroke on January 18, 1948, and was under the care of the Department of Veterans Affairs until March 11, during which period he received one hundred per cent pay and allowances. He left the hospital totally disabled and is unlikely to recover. Here is a veteran with twenty years of continuous service in the permanent force, yet. the pension board has reduced his pension from one hundred per cent to forty per cent.
Here is what they ruled in his case, and I quote the exact words:
1.	Incurred during permanent force service Canada, not pensionable as it did not arise out of nor was it directly connected' with such military service, pre-enlistment to active force service, aggravated two-fifths during that service in Canada. Effective from date of A.F. discharge.
2.	Incurred during permanent force service Canada but not pensionable as they did not arise out of nor were they directly connected with such service, pre-enlistment to active force service, not aggravated during that service.
I say the findings in this case are absurd. Here is a man with twenty years of service in the Canadian permanent force and another thirteen years in the imperial army; yet they claim his disability is not directly attributable to that service. As it stands now, if this man died today his pension would cease, since the pension commission has reduced his disability from one hundred per cent to forty per cent, and his widow would be left penniless. That is a point I cannot emphasize too strongly.
In view of this particular case, and to avoid bringing up similar cases, I would recommend to the minister that in all cases dealing with permanent force N.C.O.'s and other ranks for pension purposes, a senior ranking permanent force officer, appointed perhaps by the adjutant general, fully versed in the Pension Act, should be present when the case is considered by the pension commission. I hope the minister sees my point. This man was employed by His Majesty's government for over twenty years. His case was dealt with by the pension commission, and I believe that when a member of the permanent force has his case reviewed by that board there should be some person from the permanent force there to speak on his behalf.

Such a man, even if he were single, who is in receipt of helplessness allowance under this bill will receive $1,128 on his 100 per cent pension, $1,400 if he is totally helpless, or a total of $2,528. If he should be married, that amount will be $2,900; and if he should have a large family of four children, it would be $3,596.
Statements relating to the cost of living were made by a number of speakers. Those I admit right away. I admit the point that was made in committee with regard to the rise in the living standard as compared with that in the early days of the old veteran in the 1920's. The young people who have come from this war have entered upon a new living standard which the old-timers knew nothing about. I admit the high wages of unskilled labour and of all labour. I also admit that it is difficult to find living accommodation and that living is overly expensive where some of

our pensioners are perforce living-and by desire-in the large cities of Canada. But against that picture, black as it was sometimes painted yesterday, I should like to place a few facts that have not been mentioned in this house. I should like to mention them in all fairness to our objective in this bill, namely, to raise the morale of the pensioner and to give him a more adequate living.
All pensions are exempt from income tax. That has not always been true but it is true at the present time. You may ask how income tax will affect the pensioner. I will refer to that later on, because we have many pensioners paying income tax. There is free medical treatment for pensioners with hospital allowance, with the provision of free appliances if they need them because of their disabilities. There is a stability of basic income through the ups and downs of our economic picture into the future, at least as far as we can see it today. I am far happier about this bill based upon an increase in basic rates than I would be, I was going to say, about almost any other. But at least I would hate to see ihc increase entirely based upon something that was tied solidly to the cost of living index. These are men who want to know as nearly as they can what this backlog of income will be this year, next year and the year after, and to be able to govern themselves accordingly. The stability factor is, to my mind, a valuable one. We are now at the peak height. Eight years from now we know not where that point will be, but this award will, I hope, not fall below this level for a great many years.
There is a disability preference in the civil service which places the pensioner not only above the ordinary applicants but above the other veterans. There is something else which is not so obvious. It is not covered by law. There is a growing preference within industry for the pensioned man. It came about through a new understanding and a new sympathy on the part of industry, if you like. Then it was clinched by the fact that it was found that normally the pensioned man, in the specific role which applied to him, often does a better job than the fit man would, which seems unbelievable, but has been demonstrated.
Pensioners are subsidized through the workman's compensation acts of the provinces by virtue of the fact that when a pensioner in industry is hurt, we pay the costs. There is, therefore, a reasonable security, and I consider this rather important. I have here somewhere what it would mean in dollars and cents on an annuity basis, but I will not quote from it. I will just state the simple fact that the

Pension Act
pensioner has a reasonable security for his dependents without cost to himself. He has security by way of provision for his widow where the disability is 50 per cent or over, and also on the matter of employment, which is related to that point of income tax.
Following some of the discussion yesterday, and speaking of the seriously disabled men who were pensioned, particularly those in the helplessness group, men who have worked hard during the years to get back their independence, to reassure themselves that they can be producers and citizens in the full sense, I feel that we ought always to watch how we can encourage them. Within the department, we have a 100 per cent pensioner who would qualify for helplessness allowance; he is director of our casualty rehabilitation section. He is an inspiration to the men with whom he is working. This is a section about which we do not send out much publicity. It is one about which we do not talk a great deal, and that is done deliberately. He advises me that the men like himself do not want to be held up for pity. They do not want their great disabilities to be over-emphasized. They like to have unostentatious assistance and perhaps the best assistance comes when they know not how it comes. This technique which he has developed within his section of the department is something that was, to me, a surprising factor in its success.
I should like to add that the director of prosthetic services is himself a total disability pensioner, having lost both legs and one eye. Throughout the work that is being carried out by men comparable with those I have mentioned, in the 75 per cent to 100 per cent pension group, and in the whole of the helplessness allowance group, we have only approximately six per cent who are not either under treatment or under training for rehabilitation or who have not employment. There are only about six per cent who are not employed or under appropriate treatment or training. To my mind that is an outstanding achievement, and when the estimates of my department are brought into the house, if I were called upon to delete from them the amount necessary to continue that rehabilitation work, I would feel much sorrier about cutting it out than I am at not being able to increase pensions by 33^ per cent. I thought I would mention that.
With respect to what has been said, I have just been handed by the chairman of the committee an item in today's Evening Citizen of Ottawa, appearing under the heading:
Legion approves 25 per cent boost in vets' pensions
Approval of the 25 per cent increase in pensions for veterans now before the House of
Commons was expressed by Major General C. B. Price, dominion president of the Canadian Legion.
The legion head in a statement said:
"All branches of the legion will be gratified by the recent announcement by the Minister of Veterans Affairs in the House of Commpns, that the recommendations of the parliamentary committee respecting amendments to the pension bill are being accepted.
"This is a very satisfactory culmination of two years of effort by the legion to bring pern sion rates into line with present day conditions 

no revision having been made since 1925.
Non-Partisan
"Ever since 1919 parliament has dealt with veterans' affairs on a non-partisan basis, and we particularly appreciate the effective work accomplished by the parliamentary committee and the splendid contributions to the results made by all parties represented in the House of Commons.
"It is also gratifying that the government has accepted the unanimous recommendation of the committee for a twentydive per cent increase for all beneficiaries under the Pension Act and also the recommendation for an almost 100 per cent increase in helplessness allowances."

I have argued in this house for many years that, in any section of the country, where the pensioner who may be 10 per cent disabled from a medical point of view seeks employment, if there is nothing but heavy industry in that section of the country, for employment purposes that man is 100 per cent disabled, and that is more pronounced today than ever. Almost all the unemployed in my particular area are veterans of this war; and the steel and coal companies, and I believe every heavy industry across the country, have adopted the practice of having men medically examined before they are employed. One of the first things the ex-service man is confronted with when he seeks employment is the fact that he is five, ten, fifteen or twenty per cent disabled, and they are not hiring anyone who is not 100 per cent fit. In addition, they have closed down completely on hiring anyone who is over forty years of age.
If the minister has been led to believe that the statement he just made is applicable to all industry across this country, I cannot sit here without saying to him that I know this is a burning question all through Nova Scotia, where there are hundreds of men with disabilities of five, ten, fifteen or twenty per cent who cannot get work. speechtext:
Even if the minister does not like it, I would point out that it is the purpose of a pension act to compensate people for disabilities they have suffered in the service of their country, and to give them something as near as possible to the average of the standard of living of the Canadian people.
That average changes rapidly these days, in terms of dollars and cents, and fairly rapidly in terms of consumable goods and services. While I supported the motion to increase the amount by 33J per cent, when the matter was before the committee, I still feel that a cost of living bonus on top of the floor amount would be better. If 33 j per cent was the proper amount of increase-and it was considered the proper amount by many people across the country who have given the matter serious thought-and if $100 a month was the amount necessary to meet the cost of living at that time, at an index of 150 8, we may take it as axiomatic that the 150-8 cost of living index equals $100 a month, the amount considered sufficient for a single person to provide that type of living which we should be prepared to provide for those who have been hurt in our service.
This being so, I felt, and still feel, that by granting an increase of 25 per cent, to strike a figure below which a pension could never drop-and that would be $94 a month-it would equal a cost of living index of 144. So you would have $1 for each point in the cost of living, which would bring it to $100 a month at that time. It has since gone up a point, so it would require to be $101 a month now.
The point I make is that $94 a month will not likely ever again be more than sufficient to provide a bare existence. I do not know whether we shall have a depression. Some say we shall, and others say we shall not. I think so too-whichever way you wish to take it. I do not know, nor does anyone else. There is good reason to suppose, however, that there might be an increase in the cost of living when the Marshall plan goes into effect, and when the Minister of Finance really gets down to business and gives effect to this 25 per cent.
All those things can happen. So far as I can see, however-and many agree with me- there would not seem to be a time within the conceivable future when $94 a month would be too much. Therefore, by taking a base of $94, and never allowing it to go below that figure; and by taking the cost of living bonus on top of that we would, I believe, give the veteran a reasonable assurance that he would have something above a mere existence all the way through.

North Fraser Harbour Commissioners Act
The matter of wage increases has been mentioned. Perhaps they are a good guide. In committee we had a plethora of charts and tables prepared by experts. These were a good guide. But the actual fact is that we are trying to compensate people who have been hurt. We are1 not trying to pay people for a production job they are doing now. They have done their production job and have suffered in the process; and it is my view that they should have a definite assurance that they will never again have to suffer physically because of their living conditions if the country can prevent it.
I believe, therefore, that from now until we meet again the government should give consideration to this idea and bring in something along these lines which will give the assurance I have indicated. I feel strongly about the cost of living bonus and always will.

subtopic: NORTH FRASER-SUBSTITUTION OF CITY OF VANCOUVER FOR MUNICIPALITIES OF SOUTH VANCOUVER AND POINT GREY

speechtext:
Hon. LIONEL CHEVRIER (Minister of Transport) moved the second reading of Bill No. 208, to amend the North Fraser Harbour Commissioners Act.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, by 3-4 George V,
chapter 162, there was incorporated the North Fraser Harbour Commissioners. One amendment has been made to that act, and this bill proposes to make another one of a noncontentious variety. It is brought about in this manner. In 1929 the municipalities of South Vancouver and Point Grey were united with the city of Vancouver. The purpose of the bill is to substitute the city of Vancouver for the municipalities of South Vancouver and Point Grey and thereby remove the anomaly now existing.

subtopic: NORTH FRASER-SUBSTITUTION OF CITY OF VANCOUVER FOR MUNICIPALITIES OF SOUTH VANCOUVER AND POINT GREY
speechtext: What is the anomaly?

subtopic: NORTH FRASER-SUBSTITUTION OF CITY OF VANCOUVER FOR MUNICIPALITIES OF SOUTH VANCOUVER AND POINT GREY
speechtext:
The anomaly is that the two municipalities have been incorporated within the city of Vancouver, and it is proposed to change the names of South Vancouver and Point Grey to the municipality of the city of Vancouver. It is a simple amendment.
The commission consists of three commissioners, two of whom are appointed by the governor in council and one by resolution passed by the four municipalities. If this bill carries there will be but two municipalities. A request for this amendment was made by the city of Vancouver in 1942 but was not carried out because of the war. Since then, letters have been received from the clerks of the municipalities of Burnaby and Richmond and the corporation council of the city of Vancouver and from solicitors for the North Fraser harbour commissioners, approving the proposed amendments. The changes made by the other sections of the bill are necessary in order to make similar substitutions.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, considered in committee, read the third time and passed.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
There is not a great deal more that we can say on this bill in addition to what was said on the resolution. We in this party are not prepared to accept this amendment to the National Housing Act as being an effective remedy to the housing crisis in Canada. I want to say a few words with respect to it.
This is an expedient along the pathway of housing in Canada; but, as we have said before, it is only one item in this field of trial and error that the government has started on. The main and probably only real feature of the bill is the element of rental insurance, but I would point out that that feature covers a narrow field. The minister has said it is intended to cover only the moderate rental field; in other words, rentals around the level of 880 a month or less. The areas in which the housing may be built are restricted and no project will be considered unless it covers eight or more family housing units. The type of building, the size and type of rooms and so on are all subject to restriction and control by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
It cannot be said that this bill meets in any way the need for veterans housing, because we cannot expect that veterans will be in position to pay $80 a month or thereabouts. In so far as housing and the primary responsibility of the government are concerned, this bill does not touch the problem at all.
In October last year the minister stated that some 12,000 wartime housing units would be provided throughout the country. A great deal [DOT]of interest was taken in the minister's statement, but it turns out that, of that number, only some 3,500 have been proceeded with by Wartime Housing, while about 5,200 are under negotiation. Earlier this year a statement was given out by the Department of Trade and Commerce that negotiations had been com-

menced with some seventy-nine municipalities which goes to show the interest there is in the country in veterans housing.
There are small and large communities among those seventy-nine. There are small places like Aylmer and Barrie and cities like Belleville; there are places like Bowmanville and so on. Brockville wanted 100 houses, Burlington wanted twenty-five and Chesley wanted fifty. The fact of the matter is that these municipalities have problems of their own. Taxation is a problem with them, because they can go only so far with respect to the money they can spend on housing. So we come back to the same old problem we have discussed before, that this matter requires the co-operation of the three levels of government in order that Wartime Housing, which is now being taken over by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation may succeed. Right now it would seem that the government is at an impasse in respect of veterans housing, and Bill No. 280 will not, in my opinion, solve the problem in any way, shape or form, so that some other means will have to be looked to.
The bill provides that lending institutions may lend up to 85 per cent of the value of the project, and in this bill lending institutions are being asked for the first time to provide the funds alone, not in co-operation or jointly with His Majesty. The fact of the matter is that the minister has so little faith in the bill himself that there is a clause in it that if the lending institutions do not come forward with the money, Central Mortgage and Housing may provide the funds.
There has been a good deal of criticism in the papers lately by lending institutions of government policies in respect of housing. I remember being at probably the first meeting that was held by the lending institutions, five or six years ago, to discuss their responsibilities with regard to housing. At that particular time they were saying to themselves: There is some responsibility on us, too, in this housing field, and we must accept some share of that responsibility. After a period of some two or three years, Housing Enterprises, in which they were all interested, was the result. That, of course, was not a success and they withdrew from the field. Now they are saying to the government: We do not like the manner in which you are carrying on these housing projects; we do not like the small down payments that are being allowed in respect of houses built under N.H.A. and Integrated Housing. Mr. R. H. Reid, president of Dominion Mortgage and Investment Associa-

National Housing Act
tioix had some highly critical things to say about the housing program of this government, but I shall not take time to quote his remarks. The fact of the matter is that the lending institutions are not taking very much interest in lending money under these government housing projects, and I think we can take it that not much help can be expected from them under this new project of rental insurance. So the matter is right back on the doorstep of the government, and Central Mortgage and Housing will probably have to carry on alone the lending of money under this project. It will have to bear the full weight of it, if it is to succeed. Under the only other project which the government brought forward by an amendment to the National Housing Act last year, only 574 units were built.
I do not wish to deal with the sections of the bill on the second reading except to make reference to section 3, which provides for loans to limited dividend housing companies. That is dealt with only in a cursory sort of way, but it is a section of the act which I think should receive careful study. We find that the government of Ontario have been quite prepared to assist the municipalities in financing the re-development of certain sections of cities and towns, and they have put up a considerable amount of money for that purpose. That is a most important factor in the housing situation today, and it brings me to the question of slum clearance.
I am all in favour of this government taking some part in slum clearance in towns and municipalities. I am all in favour of this government taking a more active interest in respect of limited dividend companies which have been mooted but for some reason have not been proceeded with. What we are all waiting for in respect of these projects is some leadership from the government. We all admit that emergency housing is something that must go, and if we are to do away with emergency housing we must have something else to take its place. I do not think rental insurance can take its place at all.
This year we have an estimated surplus of
8800.000. 000.	Why cannot we appropriate
850.000.	000 or $100,000,000 of that surplus and do something with respect to the housing problem? We talk about public investment; and the minister will tell us that some day, at the appropriate time, he is going to use some of this government money for public investment. But under our financial system, if you have a surplus in 1947 and do not use it, that is the end of the surplus; it is gone
for all time to come. We must find some ivay of appropriating some portion of those funds to carry on housing projects not only this year but next year and in the years to come.
There is one ray of hope in respect of housing. I was in Hamilton looking at some houses a few weeks ago, and I saw there just as nice a little bungalow as one could ever see, a whole row of them, erected for veterans by builders m the city of Hamilton on land that had been provided by the city. They cost $4,800 and the veteran could carry that house for $23 a month. There is not much likely to happen to a veteran who can get a house like that at that price and carry it for $23 a month. Not far away in the same city I saw another small house built on a fifty-foot lot, and of good depth. It was a five room house, with every convenience and appointment that a house could have, and was selling for $5,600. In that case also the city of Hamilton provided the land free to the veteran. That house could be carried for something like $35 a month. It is a house that any member of this House of Commons would be glad to live in.
That only goes to show what can be done with a little bit of co-operation. The city of Hamilton has co-operated with the builders and has provided the land and certain municipal services, and the veterans in Hamilton are getting the benefit of that co-operation. We find, when we get down to the root of the matter, that the reason why these houses could be built more cheaply in Hamilton was that there was competition in the trades. When a builder wanted a plumber there was not only one plumber to call on, but three or four plumbers were willing to put in a tender, and so prices in Hamilton have been kept down. The same methods could be followed in other parts of this country.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I say that this bill, in my opinion, will not provide as it should for the veterans; and if it does not, it is up to the government to bring down further amendments to the act which will work in the interests of the veteran. I say that this bill will not provide anything more than a very few housing units in 1948, probably one hundred to two hundred units, and that is not good enough.

speechtext:
I think it was significant, Mr. Speaker, that the minister who is piloting this legislation through the house did not take advantage of the usual opportunity to make some comments in connection with the bill. I might mention that
National Housing Act

my deskmate, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), speaking on May 6, as reported at page 3695 of Hansard said this:
Coming as I do from a city where the housing problem is a serious one, I felt that I should be taking part in this debate; but when I consider the seriousness of the housing problem and the complete failure of the government to give leadership, the emptiness of this legislation is so apparent that so far as I am concerned, it is not worth talking about.
I gather that the hon. member who has just taken his seat feels pretty much as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre does about the legislation. But the housing situation is so critical that I think some of us must say something about it, and offer our protest that the minister has not seen fit to act on the suggestions made when the resolution was before us and bring in a bill that offered some greater hope to the people of Canada.
The other day I mentioned that I should like some additional information with regard to the operations of Housing Enterprises Limited. I must thank the president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for having sent me such complete information on such short notice. The information I have -confirms my opinion that houses of the type built by Housing Enterprises Limited can be financed by an extremely small section of the Canadian people. As was mentioned By the minister the other day, the average -cost will be slightly over $8,000 per unit. Although the return gives the total as $26,326,420, and mentions that the final cost will possibly vary one per cent up or down, most builders these days find that the final costs are certainly higher than the estimated costs. I gather, therefore, that the final cost would be over $8,000 per unit.
I understand that a new formula is being used by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in determining rents. I have the rents that are being charged in the different cities, and they are low, considering the investment. I am sure that no private builders anywhere in Canada will build structures of this type and rent them at these rentals. I will not take the time to discuss all the units, but I should like to compare a few of them with the information that was disclosed at the time of the last census in 1941.
In Vancouver there are two projects. In "A" there were 136 units, built at a cost of $6,566. The rents run at $43, $45, $53, and $55. I find that, when the last census was taken, the average value of owned homes in the city of Vancouver was $3,090. The Vancouver people

were strong on mortgages, as were people in all parts of the country. Forty-one per cent of the homes had mortgages averaging $1,650 each. The monthly rent paid by the people in Vancouver in 1941 was $26. There is a fairly wide variation between the average of $26 which was paid in 1941 and the amounts that are being charged here.
The other project in Vancouver is not quite so expensive. The 213 units were built at an average cost of $5,550, but still the rents are high. They are $45, $50, $52.50 and so on up to $65. I might mention in passing that, although there is quite a wide variation in the costs of the houses built by Housing Enterprises Limited in the various cities of Canada, there does not seem to be a wide variation in the rentals.
I now come to Victoria. Costs are higher there. There were 104 units built, at an average cost of $8,675. The rents range from $45 to $60. The two-bedroom units rent at $45 and $46.50. At the time of the 1941 census the average value of owned homes in Victoria was $3,200. Only 24 per cent of the owners were the proud possessors of mortgages. The average mortgage was $1,232, and the monthly average rent was $23. I am sorry I have not the file-

speechtext:
Yes. I mentioned the average monthly rent. I am glad the minister has brought this to my attention. But even if that is taken into account, there is still a wide difference. If the average rental of unfurnished houses in Victoria was only $23 in 1941, it would be difficult for the people in those brackets to step up to rents ranging from $45 to $60.
In Saskatoon the average cost for fifty units was $7,448. In 1941 the average value of the owned houses was $2,610. There were 27 per cent with mortgages averaging $1,261. The average rent was $23 a month.
Calgary had 104 units costing an average of $7,709. In 1941 the average value of owned

National Housing Act
homes there was $3,391. Only 27 per cent had mortgages averaging $1,380. The average monthly rental was $27.
Housing costs were higher in Edmonton. In that city 106 units were built, at an average cost of $8,398. The average value of owned homes in Edmonton in 1941 was $2,879. Twenty-one per cent had mortgages averaging $989. The average monthly rent was $26.
Coming to London, Ontario, we find the costs are away up. For 186 units the average cost was $8,467. In 1941 the average value of the owned homes was $3,550. Of these 41 per cent had mortgages averaging $1,588. The average monthly rent was $29.
Hamilton, Ontario, had 116 units built by Housing Enterprises, costing an average of $6,826, with rents ranging from $42 to $55. The average value of owned homes in Hamilton in 1941 was $3,898, with 56 per cent of the people owning mortgages averaging $1,890. The average rent was $27 a month.
In Kitchener, Ontario, the average cost of 114 units was $7,577. The rents ranged from $42 to $57. In 1941 the average value of owned homes was $4,257, with 63 per cent having mortgages averaging $1,899. The monthly average rent was $27.
Brantford had fifty-four units built at an average cost of $7,889. The average value of the owned homes in 1941 was $3,627. The percentage with mortgages was 43-6; the average mortgage was $1,443. The monthly average rent was $23.
In Toronto the costs are the highest in Canada. There were two projects. One was Danforth court, where thirty-three units were built, at an average cost of $10,527. Then in Greenwood court, thirty-seven units were built, at an average cost of $10,637. The average value of owned homes in Toronto in 1941 was $4,684; the percentage with mortgages 59-5; the average mortgage, $2,323; the monthly average rent, $35.
In Montreal, taking the Villeray terrace, there are 150 houses, the cost being $5,856; and there are the Benny Farm Gardens, $8,827. I am not familiar with either of these projects, but there is quite a wide variation in costs, running from $5,856, with rentals at from $10 to $45, and $8,827, with rentals at from $62.50 to $89. In 1941 the average value of owned homes was $3,937 and the monthly average rent was $26. The average mortgage on mortgaged homes was $2,191.
In Three Rivers there were fifty-seven houses, the value being $9,065, with rents
running from $44 to $57. In 1941 the average value of owned homes was $3,062, 43 per cent with mortgages, the average mortgage on mortgaged homes being $1,521, and the average rent being $22 a month.
In Saint John there were 106 units averaging $7,517, the average value of owned homes in 1941 being $2,415, and the percentage of homes with mortgage 26-2. The average mortgage on mortgaged homes was $995, and the average monthly rent $22.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the first responsibility of the government should not be to provide housing accommodation for people in the higher income brackets, people who can pay higher rents, people who would have found some means of securing living accommodation even if the Canadian people had not spent $26,000,000 on housing.
When I was discussing the resolution in committee the other day the minister asked me where I had got my information to support my contention that there was a very small percentage of the Canadian people who could pay rents of this sort. At that time I did not have the "National Accounts Income and Expenditure, 1938-1945," but I have it with me now. It is published under the authority of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. These figures are for 1942, but I checked this morning to see whether there was not more up-to-date information. The minister may tell me that the incomes are higher than they were in 1942, but it is not my fault that I have not the figures.

speechtext:
But even making allowances for the fact that incomes have gone up since 1942, you still find from the statistics that there is only a small percentage of the Canadian people in receipt of incomes that would warrant the payment of the sort of rents that have to be paid. On page 35 of the "National Accounts Income and Expenditure," giving the distribution of income recipients by income classes in Canada, 1942, twenty per cent of the married men in Canada in that year were getting less than 81,000 a year. There were fifty per cent getting less than $2,000 a year. There were only three per cent of the married men who were getting over $5,000. Even if there are -twice as many now who are getting over $5,000, you still have only six per cent of the people getting over $5,000 a year; *and with such a large number in these low-income brackets, what the minister should be bringing in now is a plan to provide large-scale low-rental houses, so that the people who are living in these slum areas might look forward, in one or two or five years, to moving out of such slums and into modern fireproofed houses.
I have argued before, from the point of view of the people as a whole, that it would be cheaper to demolish the slums and provide low-rental housing, subsidized, in a good environment, than to maintain prisons, the high cost of fire protection necessitated by the present conditions, the high cost of hospital care, and so forth.
